simulation: Simulation: a browser cannot run a real traceroute. The routes are prepared, starting from an assumed home connection in Frankfurt am Main, with addresses reserved for examples. The times are not measured, but they are honest: no hop is faster than light in glass fibre allows.
intro: A connection is a chain of machines, and every link costs time. traceroute sends packets with a growing lifetime: every router on the way takes one off, and where it reaches zero, that router reports back. So every hop gives itself away - with its name and the time there and back.
mapped: There is no route of its own for "{host}". The simulation shows the prepared route "{route}" instead - the way there would look much like it.
unknownHost: "{host}" is neither a valid host name nor an IPv4 address.

roles.subsea: At the far end of a subsea cable
roles.silent: A router that does not answer

silentNote: Many network operators switch off the reply to traceroute. The packet still gets through.
summary: {hops, plural, one {# hop} other {# hops}}, {ms, number, ::.0} ms to the destination and back.
jump: The biggest jump in time comes between hop {from, number} and {to, number}: plus {delta, number, ::.0} ms.

why.lan: Inside your own network the way is a single hop, and the reply comes back in under a millisecond.
why.ispAccess: Most of the time goes on the first stretch: the line from your router to your provider. After that it runs over fast fibre, and the website is delivered by a server close by.
why.subsea: Here the packet crosses an ocean through a subsea cable. Light in glass fibre needs about 5 ms per 1000 km - twice that there and back. No router can shorten that time.
why.carrier: Here the packet covers a long distance over land. There too, distance is what sets the time.
